QF.id: Clubbing, Set-Off and Carry Forward of Losses_15

question.text: Mr. Ajay transferred Rs.8,00,000 to his wife Neha who invested it in mutual funds. The mutual fund generated income of Rs.50,000 in Year 1 (clubbed with Ajay). In Year 2, Neha reinvested the Rs.50,000 income into another mutual fund which earned Rs.4,000. Whose income is the Rs.4,000 in Year 2?

answer.text: Ajay's income, as the original transfer was without consideration
Neha's income, as income arising from accretion (income on income) belongs to the transferee
Split equally between Ajay and Neha
Exempt from tax as it is indirect income from a gift

explanation.text: The Logic: Under spouse-transfer clubbing, only the income arising directly from the transferred asset is clubbed with the transferor. The Rs.50,000 earned in Year 1 from the mutual fund bought with Ajay's Rs.8,00,000 is therefore correctly clubbed with Ajay. When Neha reinvests that already-clubbed Rs.50,000 into a separate mutual fund, the Rs.4,000 she earns in Year 2 is "income on income" or income from accretion — it is income on Neha's own asset (the Rs.50,000 income that became her property after taxation), not from the original transferred asset, and so it belongs to Neha and is taxed in her hands. The Trap: Option A would extend clubbing perpetually to all downstream income, which the law does not do — clubbing catches only the first layer. A 50:50 split (Option C) has no basis in the clubbing provisions. Option D treats the income as fully exempt, but income on income is fully taxable, just in the transferee's hands. Note: The cited NISM Series X-B Investment Adviser Level 2 workbook pages reviewed in the audit support first-layer spouse asset-transfer clubbing by example, but the specific "income on income / accretion" rule used to assign the Year 2 Rs.4,000 to Neha is not on the pages checked. The framing above reflects general Income Tax Act jurisprudence on clubbing.
